- As you can see, the processing started with collect() - This is the lazy initialization that spark uses. Even though you had map and reduceByKey, the process kicked off at collect. As map and reduceByKey are transformations You can see 3 partitions and each having a task - since you initialized RDD with 3 partitions Another point is how each of map and reduceByKey handled data locality. All three tasks in map have PROCESS_LOCAL. The reduceByKey needs a data shuffle and so you might have PROCESS_LOCAL and NODE_LOCAL.

Answers:
- This is a common problem. The cost of creating a connection can dwarf the actual work you're doing. In Cloud Bigtable, you can set google.bigtable.use.cached.data.channel.pool to true in your configuration settings. That would significantly improve performance. Cloud Bigtable ultimately uses a single HTTP/2 end point for all of your Cloud Bigtable instances. I don't know of a similar construct in HBase, but one way to do this would would suggest creating an implementation of Connection that creates a single cached Connection under the covers. You would have to set the hbase.client.connection.impl to your new class.

Title:
HBase-Spark Connector: connection to HBase established for every scan?

Description:
I am using Cloudera's HBase-Spark connector to do intensive HBase or BigTable scans. It works OK, but looking at Spark's detailed logs, it looks like the code tries to re-establish a connection to HBase with every call to process the results of a Scan() which I do via the JavaHBaseContext.foreachPartition() . Am I right to think that this code re-establishes a connection to HBase every time? If so, how can I re-write it to make sure I reuse the already established connection? Here's the full sample code that produces this behavior: import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.client.ConnectionFactory; import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.client.Connection; import org.apache.hadoop.conf.Configuration; import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.HBaseConfiguration; import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.TableName; import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.client.Result; import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.client.Scan; import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.filter.FilterList; import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.filter.FirstKeyOnlyFilter; import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.filter.KeyOnlyFilter; import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.filter.PageFilter; import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.filter.PrefixFilter; import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.io.ImmutableBytesWritable; import org.apache.hadoop.hbase.spark.JavaHBaseContext; import org.apache.spark.SparkConf; import org.apache.spark.api.java.JavaRDD; import org.apache.spark.api.java.JavaSparkContext; import org.apache.spark.api.java.function.VoidFunction; import scala.Tuple2; import java.util.Iterator; public class Main { public static void main(String args[]) throws Exception { SparkConf sc = new SparkConf().setAppName(Main.class.toString()).setMaster("local"); Configuration hBaseConf = HBaseConfiguration.create(); Connection hBaseConn = ConnectionFactory.createConnection(hBaseConf); JavaSparkContext jSPContext = new JavaSparkContext(sc); JavaHBaseContext hBaseContext = new JavaHBaseContext(jSPContext, hBaseConf); int numTries = 5; byte rowKey[] = "ffec939d-bb21-4525-b1ff-f3143faae2".getBytes(); for(int i = 0; i < numTries; i++) { Scan s = new Scan(rowKey); FilterList fList = new FilterList(FilterList.Operator.MUST_PASS_ALL); Answers:
- This is a common problem. The cost of creating a connection can dwarf the actual work you're doing. In Cloud Bigtable, you can set google.bigtable.use.cached.data.channel.pool to true in your configuration settings. That would significantly improve performance. Cloud Bigtable ultimately uses a single HTTP/2 end point for all of your Cloud Bigtable instances. I don't know of a similar construct in HBase, but one way to do this would would suggest creating an implementation of Connection that creates a single cached Connection under the covers. You would have to set the hbase.client.connection.impl to your new class.

Answers:
- This is a common problem. The cost of creating a connection can dwarf the actual work you're doing. In Cloud Bigtable, you can set google.bigtable.use.cached.data.channel.pool to true in your configuration settings. That would significantly improve performance. Cloud Bigtable ultimately uses a single HTTP/2 end point for all of your Cloud Bigtable instances. I don't know of a similar construct in HBase, but one way to do this would would suggest creating an implementation of Connection that creates a single cached Connection under the covers. You would have to set the hbase.client.connection.impl to your new class.

Answers:
- As you can see, the processing started with collect() - This is the lazy initialization that spark uses. Even though you had map and reduceByKey, the process kicked off at collect. As map and reduceByKey are transformations You can see 3 partitions and each having a task - since you initialized RDD with 3 partitions Another point is how each of map and reduceByKey handled data locality. All three tasks in map have PROCESS_LOCAL. The reduceByKey needs a data shuffle and so you might have PROCESS_LOCAL and NODE_LOCAL.

Answers:
- This is a common problem. The cost of creating a connection can dwarf the actual work you're doing. In Cloud Bigtable, you can set google.bigtable.use.cached.data.channel.pool to true in your configuration settings. That would significantly improve performance. Cloud Bigtable ultimately uses a single HTTP/2 end point for all of your Cloud Bigtable instances. I don't know of a similar construct in HBase, but one way to do this would would suggest creating an implementation of Connection that creates a single cached Connection under the covers. You would have to set the hbase.client.connection.impl to your new class.

I am using Cloudera's HBase-Spark connector to do intensive HBase or BigTable scans. Am I right to think that this code re-establishes a connection to HBase every time? If so, how can I re-write it to make sure I reuse the already established connection? Answers:
- This is a common problem. The cost of creating a connection can dwarf the actual work you're doing. In Cloud Bigtable, you can set google.bigtable.use.cached.data.channel.pool to true in your configuration settings. That would significantly improve performance. Cloud Bigtable ultimately uses a single HTTP/2 end point for all of your Cloud Bigtable instances. I don't know of a similar construct in HBase, but one way to do this would would suggest creating an implementation of Connection that creates a single cached Connection under the covers. You would have to set the hbase.client.connection.impl to your new class.

Thank you username_1 for your support.
- Let me close the issue as solved.

But .. First Option (if you want only to see the transformation): >>> rdd.reduceByKey(lambda x,y: x+y).collect() [(u'a', 1), (u'lamb', 2), (u'little', 1), (u'white', 1), (u'had', 1), (u'fleece', 1), (u'The', 1), (u'snow,', 1), (u'Everywhere', 1), (u'went', 1), (u'was', 2), (u'the', 2), (u'as', 1), (u'go,', 1), (u'sure', 1), (u'lamb,', 1), (u"It's", 1), (u'yeah', 2), (u'to', 1), (u'child', 1), (u'Mary', 1)] Second Option (if you want to save your transformation in a new rdd): If you do this: >>> rddReduced = rdd.reduceByKey(lambda x,y: x+y) And then this: >>> rddReduced.collect() [(u'a', 1), (u'lamb', 2), (u'little', 1), (u'white', 1), (u'had', 1), (u'fleece', 1), (u'The', 1), (u'snow,', 1), (u'Everywhere', 1), (u'went', 1), (u'was', 2), (u'the', 2), (u'as', 1), (u'go,', 1), (u'sure', 1), (u'lamb,', 1), (u"It's", 1), (u'yeah', 2), (u'to', 1), (u'child', 1), (u'Mary', 1)] You have applied and saved your transformation, the result is what you were looking for. The same concept if you want to apply sortByKey()

Title:
Getting stuck in TSoF on a Spark Standalone cluster

Description:

Title:
Simple RDD jobs take very long time to finish

Description:
Question The following simple reduce job takes about 8 seconds to complete on my machine running spark locally: import pyspark sc = pyspark.SparkContext('local[*]') rdd3 = sc.parallelize(range(10)) import time s = time.time() rdd3.reduce(lambda x, y: x + y) print(time.time() - s) > 8.376211166381836 If I run the same job on a dedicated server, the task completes in some milliseconds as expected, but on my machine it takes about 8 seconds. It seems as if Spark will lose about 5 seconds for each parallel task, no matter how small. On larger files which it splits in many tasks, the process takes minutes, if not hours, while it should take only a few seconds. Anyone an idea about what could be causing this delay? Note that this delay is not only caused by a reduce job, but by most operations on RDDs (map, count, etc.) that result in multiple parallel tasks. Update: Starting pyspark ( pyspark --master local[2] ) gives similar results as above: 2,8sec, but Spark had split the job in 2 tasks this time, so the latency is of the same order. Update 2: I also tried the same with Scala cmd ( spark-shell --master local[2] ). val df = sc.parallelize(1 to 10) df.reduce((x,y) => (x+y)) This time it finished as it should: in 0,025909 sec. Title:
Spark settings

Description:
We're wanting to use SparkFlow for source detection on radio astronomy images, but even on the MNINST example jobs with larger iteration counts are failing. Given the 60,000 images in the MNINST dataset, if we split that data into train and test sets (60% 40%) we want to train on ~ 36021 images; mini batch size of 200 over 5 epochs means we need ~ 900 iterations. Job starts, executors begin processing until all but one executor fails with the error message below 19/05/06 09:26:13 INFO python.PythonRunner: Times: total = 1796882, boot = -1772, init = 1794, finish = 1796860 19/05/06 09:26:13 INFO executor.Executor: Finished task 13.0 in stage 4.0 (TID 45). 2409 bytes result sent to driver 19/05/06 09:36:16 ERROR executor.CoarseGrainedExecutorBackend: RECEIVED SIGNAL TERM 19/05/06 09:36:16 INFO storage.DiskBlockManager: Shutdown hook called 19/05/06 09:36:16 INFO util.ShutdownHookManager: Shutdown hook called Spark session configuration for the job spark2-submit \ --master yarn \ --deploy-mode client \ --executor-memory 6g \ --executor-cores 1 \ --driver-memory 12g \ --driver-cores 5 \ --conf spark.yarn.appMasterEnv.RGZ_ENV=true \ --conf spark.shuffle.service.enabled=true \ --conf spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true \ --conf spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout=600 \ --conf spark.executor.memoryOverhead=4096 \ --conf spark.driver.memoryOverhead=4096 \ --conf spark.default.parallelism=100 \ --conf spark.pyspark.python=/home/hduser/.virtualenvs/ClaRAN/bin/python \ --conf spark.pyspark.driver.python=/home/hduser/.virtualenvs/ClaRAN/bin/python \ RunSparkflowDemo.py >spark_submitPara10execs1Cpu.log 2>&1 & The MNINST data has been loaded into a partitioned PARQUET table on the underlying HDFS data store. In this example, the data frame has 14 partitions. SparkAsyncDL configuration - documentation on the partitions parameter is a little sparse, assume for best performance we match the number of partitions that the data frame has? spark_model = SparkAsyncDL( inputCol='features', tensorflowGraph=mg, tfInput='x:0', tfLabel='y:0', tfOutput='out:0', tfLearningRate=.001, partitions=14, miniBatchSize=200, miniStochasticIters=1, shufflePerIter=False, iters=900, predictionCol='predicted', labelCol='labels', verbose=1 ) Cluster is running Spark 2.4.1 and the Python version for this job is 2.7. Long term, we want to be able to use tensorflow for source finding and object classification on very large astronomical datasets (certainly in the tens or hundreds of terabytes range, and it's entirely possible possibly larger data products will be approaching petabyte size) on appropriately sized clusters. Current cluster size is - three management servers 8 vCPUs and 24GB Ram - ten worker nodes, running 16 vCPUs and 48GB Ram (no GPU cores). Assuming our understanding of the required Spark parameters (particularly the requirement for 1 cpu per executor) and SparkAsyncDL parameters (particularly the relationship between epochs, mini batches and iterations) is correct, we're not sure why the jobs keep failing; Obviously we are missing some point and if we can;t get the MNINST example running properly it'd be counter productive to try fitting an existing tensorflow application. Any assistance you could give us would be greatly appreciated. Regards Geoff

Title:
Simple RDD jobs take very long time to finish

Description:
Question The following simple reduce job takes about 8 seconds to complete on my machine running spark locally: import pyspark sc = pyspark.SparkContext('local[*]') rdd3 = sc.parallelize(range(10)) import time s = time.time() rdd3.reduce(lambda x, y: x + y) print(time.time() - s) > 8.376211166381836 If I run the same job on a dedicated server, the task completes in some milliseconds as expected, but on my machine it takes about 8 seconds. It seems as if Spark will lose about 5 seconds for each parallel task, no matter how small. On larger files which it splits in many tasks, the process takes minutes, if not hours, while it should take only a few seconds. Anyone an idea about what could be causing this delay? Note that this delay is not only caused by a reduce job, but by most operations on RDDs (map, count, etc.) that result in multiple parallel tasks. Update: Starting pyspark ( pyspark --master local[2] ) gives similar results as above: 2,8sec, but Spark had split the job in 2 tasks this time, so the latency is of the same order. Title:
Simple RDD jobs take very long time to finish

Description:
Question The following simple reduce job takes about 8 seconds to complete on my machine running spark locally: import pyspark sc = pyspark.SparkContext('local[*]') rdd3 = sc.parallelize(range(10)) import time s = time.time() rdd3.reduce(lambda x, y: x + y) print(time.time() - s) > 8.376211166381836 If I run the same job on a dedicated server, the task completes in some milliseconds as expected, but on my machine it takes about 8 seconds. It seems as if Spark will lose about 5 seconds for each parallel task, no matter how small. On larger files which it splits in many tasks, the process takes minutes, if not hours, while it should take only a few seconds. Anyone an idea about what could be causing this delay? Note that this delay is not only caused by a reduce job, but by most operations on RDDs (map, count, etc.) that result in multiple parallel tasks. Update: Starting pyspark ( pyspark --master local[2] ) gives similar results as above: 2,8sec, but Spark had split the job in 2 tasks this time, so the latency is of the same order. Update 2: I also tried the same with Scala cmd ( spark-shell --master local[2] ). val df = sc.parallelize(1 to 10) df.reduce((x,y) => (x+y)) This time it finished as it should: in 0,025909 sec. The job was split in 2 tasks here too. So the problem has to do with pyspark? - Per your description, it sounds like host 35 exhibits intermittent failures w.r.t. libhdfs.so. - @username_2 I got the root cause and fixed it now. That was because my TF and Spark runs in docker containers, the sky-DNS used for naming resolution couldn't resolve the hostname in TensorFlow. **Test** I could ping the host with command, also my other Spark program runs well with specified hostname. Then I tried to create 1 ps and 2 workers in python with the specific hostname, REPRODUCED, changed hostname to be IP address they could communicated with each other. **Reason** Kubernetes uses sky-DNS for domain name resolution which also a Kubernetes container, I assume the sky-DNS couldn't work for TensorFlow C++ program well. **Solution** Changed `socket.gethostname()` to be `socket.gethostbyname(socket.gethostname())` for the all occurrence in `TFSparkNode.py`. Thanks.

Comments:
- Per your description, it sounds like host 35 exhibits intermittent failures w.r.t. libhdfs.so. FWIW, we had to add some [code to expand the Hadoop classpath](https://github.com/yahoo/TensorFlowOnSpark/blob/7cfc8048243a9f8c83d515cd3456f712884087fd/tensorflowonspark/TFSparkNode.py#L376-L382) for Spark 2.x + JNI. So, it sounds like either: 1) this is returning slightly different classpaths on host 35 (vs. other nodes), OR 2) there's something intermittently mangling the LD_LIBRARY_PATH on that node, OR 3) something else entirely??? For 1 and 2, you can add some debug logs inside your mnist_dist.map_fun() to see what each TF process is seeing as it's environment. For 3, you can send me the full yarn.logs at anpch@example.com (preferrably with the log statements from 1 and 2) and I can take a look. And last but not least, if it's just that one node causing problems, perhaps re-imaging it as a new node might help (if that's a possibility).

- @username_2 I got the root cause and fixed it now. That was because my TF and Spark runs in docker containers, the sky-DNS used for naming resolution couldn't resolve the hostname in TensorFlow. **Test** I could ping the host with command, also my other Spark program runs well with specified hostname. Then I tried to create 1 ps and 2 workers in python with the specific hostname, REPRODUCED, changed hostname to be IP address they could communicated with each other. **Reason** Kubernetes uses sky-DNS for domain name resolution which also a Kubernetes container, I assume the sky-DNS couldn't work for TensorFlow C++ program well. **Solution** Changed `socket.gethostname()` to be `socket.gethostbyname(socket.gethostname())` for the all occurrence in `TFSparkNode.py`. Thanks.

- by the way, does 'standalone cluster' of single host read/write all result from local file system rather than hdfs? why i found operation of that involves hdfs?
- yes, [the spark standalone example](https://github.com/yahoo/TensorFlowOnSpark/wiki/GetStarted_Standalone) just uses a single node to host multiple spark executors. In that case, the local file system acts as the "distributed file system", i.e. all nodes in the cluster are able to access the same files. If you're using multiple physical hosts in spark standalone mode, you will need to use an actual distributed file system, e.g. HDFS... otherwise, each node will read/write on it's own local disk (which is most likely not what you want and can lead to issues like you're seeing). Have you been able to run the example as-is on a single host?
- Also can you try using `hdfs://default/user/ghn/mnist_model` as the path to the model dir instead of `hdfs://hadoop222:9000/user/ghn/mnist_model` in your spark-submit command line?

I have a close look at `/sbin/start-slave.sh`. [look here](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/master/sbin/start-slave.sh) line 43 gives `echo "Usage: ./sbin/start-slave.sh [options] <master>"` line 59 gives `MASTER=$1` Is this a conflict?
- This is in Spark's codebase, so if anything, it's a conflict between their documentation on line 43 vs. their implementation on line 59. That all said, these lines haven't changed in 4 years, and if you trace the code further, it actually just ends up [reconstructing the command line arguments in order again](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/master/sbin/start-slave.sh#L83)... and if you trace that further, you eventually end up at [this parsing code](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/master/core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/deploy/worker/WorkerArguments.scala#L68-L120), which does the right thing.

That said, it looks like your TF setup isn't able to read from HDFS (per the simple write example above). So, this is usually due to the LIB_HDFS and LIB_JVM setup again, so before you run that example, try: ``` export LIB_HDFS=/path/to/your/libhdfs.so export LIB_JVM=/path/to/your/libjvm.so export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$LIB_HDFS:$LIB_JVM ``` You will need to find where the `libhdfs.so` and `libjvm.so` files are located on that box. - @username_2 I got the root cause and fixed it now. That was because my TF and Spark runs in docker containers, the sky-DNS used for naming resolution couldn't resolve the hostname in TensorFlow. **Test** I could ping the host with command, also my other Spark program runs well with specified hostname. Then I tried to create 1 ps and 2 workers in python with the specific hostname, REPRODUCED, changed hostname to be IP address they could communicated with each other. **Reason** Kubernetes uses sky-DNS for domain name resolution which also a Kubernetes container, I assume the sky-DNS couldn't work for TensorFlow C++ program well. **Solution** Changed `socket.gethostname()` to be `socket.gethostbyname(socket.gethostname())` for the all occurrence in `TFSparkNode.py`. Thanks.

Title:
Simple RDD jobs take very long time to finish

Description:
Question The following simple reduce job takes about 8 seconds to complete on my machine running spark locally: import pyspark sc = pyspark.SparkContext('local[*]') rdd3 = sc.parallelize(range(10)) import time s = time.time() rdd3.reduce(lambda x, y: x + y) print(time.time() - s) > 8.376211166381836 If I run the same job on a dedicated server, the task completes in some milliseconds as expected, but on my machine it takes about 8 seconds. It seems as if Spark will lose about 5 seconds for each parallel task, no matter how small. On larger files which it splits in many tasks, the process takes minutes, if not hours, while it should take only a few seconds. Anyone an idea about what could be causing this delay? Note that this delay is not only caused by a reduce job, but by most operations on RDDs (map, count, etc.) that result in multiple parallel tasks. Update: Starting pyspark ( pyspark --master local[2] ) gives similar results as above: 2,8sec, but Spark had split the job in 2 tasks this time, so the latency is of the same order. Update 2: I also tried the same with Scala cmd ( spark-shell --master local[2] ). val df = sc.parallelize(1 to 10) df.reduce((x,y) => (x+y)) This time it finished as it should: in 0,025909 sec. The job was split in 2 tasks here too. So the problem has to do with pyspark?
